aspects.says: BLOCKED means waiting to enter or re-enter a synchronized monitor; a thread waiting for a ReentrantLock, a semaphore, a latch or a queue is parked and shows WAITING or TIMED_WAITING.
basis: section:BLOCKED Means Waiting for a synchronized Monitor; a Thread Waiting for a ReentrantLock Is WAITING

aspects.says: A notified thread goes from WAITING to BLOCKED and stays there until the notifier leaves the synchronized block, because wait() returns only once it owns the monitor again.
basis: section:A Notified Thread Is BLOCKED Until It Gets the Monitor Back

aspects.says: A thread is NEW only until start(), and once TERMINATED, after a return or an uncaught exception, it stays TERMINATED.
basis: section:getState() Is a Snapshot: Coordinate with join() or a Latch, Never by Polling a State
aspects.reason: the JVM enforces it, so a solution has no way to get it wrong except by starting a thread twice, which unit 6.1.2 covers

aspects.says: Whether a waiting thread is stuck behind another is told by what it waits for and who holds it, not by its state: an idle worker in take() and a request parked on a held ReentrantLock are both WAITING.
basis: section:BLOCKED Means Waiting for a synchronized Monitor; a Thread Waiting for a ReentrantLock Is WAITING

aspects.says: RUNNABLE covers a thread that runs, one that waits for a processor and one blocked in a native call such as a socket read, so it says nothing about CPU use.
basis: section:RUNNABLE Means the JVM Isn't Holding the Thread Back, Not That It Is Using a CPU

aspects.says: A thread that sleeps or waits for anything but wait() inside synchronized keeps the monitor, so every other caller is BLOCKED for as long as it waits.
basis: section:Spot the Problem: a Back-Off That Holds the Cache

aspects.says: getState() is a snapshot that doesn't say where a thread waits and can change between two reads, so readiness is signalled with a latch and completion with join(), never by polling a state or sleeping.
basis: section:getState() Is a Snapshot: Coordinate with join() or a Latch, Never by Polling a State

aspects.says: WAITING and TIMED_WAITING differ only in whether the wait has a timeout; neither says whether the thread is in another thread's way or holds a lock.
basis: section:A Waiting Thread Keeps Every Lock but the One It Waits On

aspects.says: A virtual thread in a socket call reports WAITING, and neither ThreadMXBean nor jcmd Thread.print lists virtual threads, while jcmd Thread.dump_to_file does.
basis: section:RUNNABLE Means the JVM Isn't Holding the Thread Back, Not That It Is Using a CPU
aspects.reason: it shows only with a real socket and the jcmd tool run against the JVM, which a graded runner keeps out of practices; module 26 covers virtual threads

aspects.says: Object.wait() releases the monitor of the object it is called on while it waits, so other threads can enter.
basis: section:Spot the Problem: a Back-Off That Holds the Cache

aspects.says: A waiting thread leaves WAITING only when another thread acts on it (notify, unpark, an interrupt) or its time runs out; setting a field it would check later wakes nothing.
basis: section:A Notified Thread Is BLOCKED Until It Gets the Monitor Back
